strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely interesting and well-motivated problem: constructing nested, weight-sharing low-rank submodels from a pretrained network in a 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' paradigm, going beyond fixed-size compression.

The theoretical analysis in the linear setting is clean and non-trivial: Theorem 4.1 (measure-zero argument via codimension of the gauge-fixing sets), Theorem 4.2 (strictly positive submodel gap for All-Subspaces Learning, derived via nuclear-norm duality and KKT analysis in Appendix B), and Theorem 4.3 (nested submodel learning recovers the truncated-SVD Pareto front) together provide real insight into why post-training selection and joint multi-submodel training fail, and why nestedness is the right constraint. Proofs in the appendix appear sound and self-contained.

Empirical evaluation spans meaningful scales: Llama-3.2-1B/3B and Llama-3.1-8B for NLP and DINOv3 ViTs up to ViT-7B/16 for CV, with consistent improvements over SVD/DataSVD + DP selection and ACIP baselines (Figs. 4-5). The DP-based (MCKP) search over per-layer sensitivity is a sensible, scalable selection procedure (O(L·K)).

The ablations are informative: activation-sample size for DataSVD (Fig. 7a), the failure of layer-independent training (Fig. 7b), the necessity of joint nested submodel training (Fig. 8), and component-wise compression heatmaps (Fig. 6) support the central design choices.
The exhaustive validation on the small MNIST setting (Sec. 3.4, 10^4 submodels) is a nice sanity check that the nested formulation can recover the Pareto front of independently trained submodels.
Limitations are discussed honestly (Sec. 7, D.4), including restricted training budget and unexplored input adaptivity.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the theory and the method as applied. The guarantees (Theorems 4.1-4.3) hold only for a single linear layer with the true target M* known; the deep-network method relies on strong, unverified assumptions (additivity of approximation errors across layers, preservation of relative ordering under subsequent training). The claim that FlexRank 'recovers the true Pareto front' is validated only on a 4-layer MNIST network; at LLM/ViT scale there is no ground-truth Pareto front, so the headline claim is not directly supported by the main experiments.

No wall-clock latency or throughput measurements are reported. For a paper explicitly targeting deployment across hardware budgets, this is a significant omission: low-rank factorized layers with small r are notorious for poor hardware efficiency compared to dense layers, and the only efficiency argument is FLOP-based (Sec. 3.5). The claimed 'performance-latency Pareto frontier' is therefore never actually measured.

Baseline coverage is narrow. Comparisons are restricted to SVD/DataSVD+DP, ACIP, and (indirectly) SVD-LLM/DRONE/ASVD; the most relevant elastic-model baselines (MatFormer/Matformer, Flextron, LLamaFlex) are not compared experimentally, and the justification (no released implementation / proprietary data for LLamaFlex) is only partially persuasive given MatFormer is a published NeurIPS method. Similarly, the claim of outperforming 'state-of-the-art compression approaches' is not tested against quantization baselines, which dominate many deployment pipelines.

Evaluation for GPT-2 uses held-out loss on a proxy dataset, and the Llama results use zero-shot commonsense accuracy only; no perplexity on standard benchmarks (e.g., WikiText/C4) or perplexity-equivalent comparisons against the cited low-rank compression methods (ASVD, SVD-LLM), making quantitative comparison with prior literature difficult.

Some methodological details are under-specified: how the mixing coefficients αk in Eq. (6) are chosen, the number of budgets K used, and variance across seeds for the main results are not clearly reported. The distillation training cost is nontrivial (up to 8 nodes for 6 days for the 8B model), and no code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility.

Several of the reported gains are modest relative to the training cost, and the mechanism behind the especially good ViT results (Sec. 5.1 attributes it to ImageNet being small enough for more epochs) suggests sensitivity to the training regime rather than a robust property of the method.

strengths: The problem — a 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' elastic model operating in a factorized (rank) space — is well motivated and clearly positioned relative to quantization, pruning, and architectural-elasticity methods (Table 2 is a useful comparative summary).

The theory section is a genuine strength: Theorems 4.1–4.3 cleanly characterize why post-training selection and all-subspaces learning fail to recover the rank-Pareto front in the linear setting, with complete proofs, and the toy experiments (Fig. 2, exhaustive Pareto front on a 4-layer MNIST model in Fig. 3) empirically corroborate the analysis.

The MNIST exhaustive-search experiment (Sec. 3.4) is a thoughtful validation design: with K^L = 10,000 submodels it directly tests whether nested weight-sharing recovers the independently trained Pareto front, which is stronger than what the formulation requires.

Experiments span a reasonable range of scales and modalities (GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B, DINOv3 ViT-L up to ViT-7B), with ablations on calibration-set size, layer-wise vs. end-to-end training, and submodel sampling.
The limitations discussion is reasonably honest about compute cost, restricted training budget, and untested input adaptivity.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees hold only for a single linear layer. The method's actual correctness rests on two strong, essentially unvalidated assumptions: additivity of approximation errors across layers (justified by analogy to quantization literature) and preservation of the importance ordering from the frozen DataSVD initialization through training. Neither is tested directly; the only end-to-end validation of the 'recovers the true Pareto front' claim is a 4-layer MNIST network, which is far from the LLM/ViT regime where the claims are made.

The headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. 'Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art compression and elasticity approaches' is not supported: the most relevant elastic methods (Flextron, LlamaFlex) are not compared (Sec. A.1), and the remaining baselines are SVD/DataSVD variants plus ACIP. The 4.2 argument that LlamaFlex is 'an instance of ASL' is a theoretical speculation, not an empirical comparison.

The 'graceful degradation' claim is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1: at 0.4× relative size, Llama-3.2-1B drops from 18.33 to 1.22 on Code and 25.69 to 13.58 on Math, and Llama-3.2-3B drops from 36.78 to 2.03 on Code. This is catastrophic, not graceful, degradation — the favorable results are concentrated in the Fig. 4/5 curves where exact numbers are not reported in tabular form.

Main results are presented only as small multi-line figures without numeric tables, making precise evaluation of the claimed margins (e.g., 'within a 5% margin' in Fig. 5) difficult; the ViT-H+/16 parameter count labeling (840M) is also non-standard.

The GPT-2 evaluation uses held-out loss on the same proxy (FineWebEdu) distribution used for distillation, which measures how well the submodel mimics the teacher on the training distribution rather than downstream capability; downstream capability is only assessed on six commonsense zero-shot tasks, which are weakly correlated with pretraining-loss-quality for compressed LLMs.

Total cost and fairness of comparison are under-specified: FlexRank training requires 8 nodes for 6 days for the 8B model, and it is unclear whether baselines (ACIP, DataSVD+distillation variants) received comparable tuning and compute. Given the 'train-once' framing, a cost-benefit accounting versus simply distilling a few discrete submodels of matched sizes is missing.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code release is mentioned, the DP formulation details are deferred to the appendix, and several hyperparameters (loss coefficients αk, budget grid, number of sampled configurations during training) are not clearly specified.

Practical relevance of low-rank factorization for LLM deployment is not fully addressed: the method requires executing two matmuls per layer, and real speedups on serving hardware (batched GEMM, kernel support) are asserted but never measured; latency measurements are absent despite the paper's deployment motivation.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely principled framing of elastic model deployment: the formalization of 'optimally elastic' models (Def. 2.1) and the analysis in Sec. 4 of why Post-Training Selection (Thm. 4.1) and All-Subspaces Learning (Thm. 4.2) fail while Nested Subspace Learning succeeds (Thm. 4.3) is a real conceptual contribution, not just an engineering trick.

The theoretical claims are validated with controlled experiments: the MNIST-scale exhaustive experiment (Sec. 3.4, 10,000 independently trained submodels) directly verifies that FlexRank recovers the true Pareto front, which is an unusually rigorous validation of the core approximation.

Empirical evaluation spans a meaningful range of modern architectures and scales (Llama-3.2-1B/3B and Llama-3.1-8B, DINOv3 ViTs up to 7B), with sensible baselines (SVD, DataSVD, ACIP) that isolate the contribution of nested training (Figs. 4-5).

The ablations are informative: the model-profile heatmaps (Fig. 6), the calibration sample-size analysis (Fig. 7a), the layer-wise vs. end-to-end training comparison (Fig. 7b), and the single-submodel baseline (Fig. 8) each target a specific design assumption of the method.
Limitations are honestly discussed (Sec. 7, D.4), including restricted training budgets and unexplored input adaptivity.
weaknesses: Despite the deployment motivation, evaluation is entirely in terms of parameter counts and FLOPs; there are no wall-clock latency or throughput measurements. Low-rank factorizations often fail to deliver real speedups on GPU/edge hardware compared to dense kernels, and this is precisely the criticism the paper levels at sparsity methods in the introduction, so the omission is significant for the central 'deploy-everywhere' claim.

The theoretical results hold only for a single linear layer with exact SVD structure and hinge on strong assumptions (additivity of approximation errors across layers, preservation of relative importance ordering after training). The paper acknowledges these assumptions but provides no theory or quantitative evidence bridging the linear analysis to deep transformers.

Comparisons with closely related elastic LLM methods (Flextron, LlamaFlex) are absent, justified only by unavailability of implementations and low-rank focus (Sec. A.1). At least a reproduced variant or a qualitative head-to-head on a common model would substantially strengthen the SOTA claim in the abstract.

The distillation training is expensive (up to 8 nodes x 6 days for the 8B model, Sec. D.4) and results are reported under a limited regime (10k steps, half an epoch); the ViT advantage is explicitly attributed to this asymmetry, which weakens generalization of the NLP conclusions.

Post-adaptation results (Tab. 1) show quite steep degradation at 0.6x and 0.4x budgets (e.g., code accuracy dropping from 18.6 to 3.3), which qualifies the 'graceful degradation' narrative at aggressive compression levels.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, and some reproducibility-relevant details (e.g., the number/spacing of budgets K, DP implementation specifics for the nested constraint) are deferred or under-specified.
The CV evaluation uses a frozen-backbone classification head as the proxy task rather than a language-modeling objective, which may not be representative of the intended LLM deployment scenario.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: inducing elasticity directly in the factorized weight space for 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' deployment is a useful and timely direction, and the paper is, to my knowledge, among the first to formalize nested submodel training in the low-rank regime.

The theoretical section is a genuine contribution: Theorems 4.1–4.3 cleanly characterize why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) fail and why nested submodel learning (NSL) recovers the Pareto front in the linear setting, with full proofs in App. B (measure-theoretic nongenericity argument, spectral interference analysis, induction on nested minimizers). These results give real insight and inform the method design.

Broad experimental coverage across architectures and scales: GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B and Llama-3.1-8B, and DINOv3 ViTs from ViT-L/16 up to ViT-7B/16, with comparisons to SVD/DataSVD, DRONE, SVD-LLM, ACIP (the SOTA elastic low-rank method), LLM-Pruner, and LayerSkip, plus a matched-budget independent-submodels baseline that isolates the benefit of weight sharing.

The ablations are thorough and well-designed: ranking-preservation of the DP probe is validated on an exhaustively searchable 10^4-submodel setting (Spearman 0.991, 94.1% exact match, low regret); Fig. 7(b) convincingly shows independent layer training fails while end-to-end consolidation works; Fig. 8 confirms the need for joint submodel training.

GAR (gauge-aligned reparametrization) is a practical contribution that avoids the dense r×r block, and the authors apply it uniformly to baselines (Remark 5.1), which is a fair-comparison practice; App. D.4 includes empirical runtime measurements supporting the theoretical cost model.
The limitations discussion (training memory/compute overhead ~2x, no adaptive routing evaluation, dependence on training data quality) is honest and specific rather than perfunctory.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the theory and the method as applied. The Theorems 4.1–4.3 concern a single linear matrix with Frobenius reconstruction loss, while the actual method operates on deep nonlinear networks with distillation loss. The key bridging assumptions (ranking preservation under an additive error probe, preservation of relative submodel optimality through training, Sec. 3.2) are empirically validated only in a tiny MNIST/CNN-MLP setting (App. C.3, D.1); no evidence is provided for these assumptions on the actual Llama/ViT experiments where the claims matter most.

Main results (Fig. 4, Fig. 5) appear to be single runs without seed variance or confidence intervals, in contrast to Table 1 which reports standard deviations. Given the modest margins over some baselines in Fig. 5 and the sensitivity of LLM zero-shot evaluations, this weakens the evidential support for 'most graceful degradation'.

Comparison fairness concerns: the matched-budget protocol is argued but each competitor is trained/tuned under a different regime; the strongest elastic baselines (FlexTron, LlamaFlex) are not compared at all (justified by missing code/proprietary data), and the concurrent rank-elasticity work of Rauba & van der Schaar (2026) is discussed but not compared. The independent-submodels baseline appears only for Llama-3.2-1B.

Deployment claims are not fully substantiated: the abstract and introduction promise 'practical inference savings' and deployment relevance, but wall-clock measurements (App. D.4, Fig. 10) cover a single matrix shape (m=n=4096) on one GPU; no end-to-end latency/throughput for actual Llama/ViT models is reported, and the GAR reparametrization with a leading identity block may interact unfavorably with real transformer kernels.

Post-adaptation results (Table 1) show significant degradation at reduced budgets (e.g., code accuracy drops from ~18-37 to ~1-7 at 0.4x), suggesting the graceful-degradation property is much weaker after downstream finetuning; the paper does not discuss this tension.

Several correctness/editorial defects: Corollary B.8 states the suboptimal solution satisfies (Û,V̂) ∈ M/:= {...}, where the proof intends non-membership (also the corollary statement contradicts its own proof sketch); App. C.1 contains a circular definition (Δθl = (Δθl − UlVl⊤)); the footnote 'Code available at' is empty, harming reproducibility despite otherwise detailed experimental appendices.

The impact of the DP nestedness constraint on solution quality is not ablated (nested chain is enforced post-hoc in Algorithm 2's NESTEDCHAIN step); the cost of dropping Pareto-optimal but non-nested configurations is not quantified on real models.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a real, underexplored problem: extracting nested, importance-ordered low-rank submodels from a pretrained model for elastic deployment, and frames it cleanly via a Pareto-elastic model definition (Sec. 2).

The linear-model theory (Sec. 4, App. B) is a genuine contribution: Theorems 4.1-4.3 give a principled explanation of why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) fail and why nested submodel learning (NSL) recovers the Pareto front, with complete proofs in the appendix.

The method is well-engineered and complete: DataSVD initialization, a DP-based nested rank-selection procedure with O(L·K) complexity (App. C.2), knowledge-consolidation distillation, and a practical Gauge-Aligned Reparametrization (GAR, Sec. 3.5) that makes low-rank inference actually cheaper, with runtime measurements (App. D.4, Fig. 10).

Experiments span GPT-2, three Llama models (up to 8B), and DINOv3 ViTs (up to 7B), with ablations on calibration sample size, layer-wise vs. end-to-end training, submodel sampling, and profile heatmaps (Sec. 5.3), plus a post-adaptation LoRA study (Tab. 1).

The DP ranking-preservation assumption is explicitly analyzed rather than hidden (App. C.3, Fig. 9), and the limitations section (Sec. 7) honestly discusses 2x training overhead, kernel issues, and untested adaptive routing.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims hold only for a single linear layer in Frobenius norm; the bridge to deep nonlinear networks rests on a strong additivity/ranking-preservation assumption that is validated only in a toy MNIST setting (10^4 submodels), not at any realistic scale. The claim that FlexRank 'recovers the true Pareto front' is therefore demonstrated only on four-layer MLP/CNNs, and should not be read as a general guarantee.

Evaluation protocol for LLMs is weak: GPT-2 is evaluated by loss on a held-out split of the same proxy dataset, and Llama results are zero-shot commonsense accuracy only, with no standard perplexity benchmarks. Fig. 4 shows absolute accuracies in the 30-55% range without error bars or seeds, making 'most graceful degradation' hard to verify rigorously.

The headline 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' framing is not compared against the strongest practical competing route: quantization (e.g., GPTQ/AWQ) is acknowledged in the intro but never empirically compared, and no end-to-end latency/throughput numbers on real models are reported — only a synthetic matrix-multiply microbenchmark (Fig. 10). Parameter counts are used as a proxy for cost throughout.

Table 1 undercuts the graceful-degradation narrative at aggressive budgets: code accuracy collapses from 18.3 to 1.22 at 0.4x on Llama-3.2-1B (and 36.8 to 2.03 on 3B), a far cry from the ViT 'within 5% up to 70% pruning' story.

The matched-budget baseline (Fig. 5) — independently training the same FlexRank-selected submodels — only 'slightly' outperforms is reversed: FlexRank beats it only marginally, and the advantage is attributed to an unverified hypothesis. This weakens the weight-sharing contribution's empirical significance.

Baseline fairness is questionable: comparisons at 'best tuning/budget' mix methods trained with vastly different data/compute (LayerSkip on 839B tokens vs. 5B here), and FlexTRON/LLamaFlex, the closest elastic alternatives, are excluded from experiments with justification limited to lack of released code (App. A.1).

Reproducibility is materially undermined: the footnote reads 'Code available at' with no URL, and several hyperparameters (e.g., the alpha_k budget weights in Eq. 6, number of sampled submodels during consolidation) are not specified in the visible text.
Presentation flaws further reduce clarity: garbled/overlapping axis labels in Fig. 2, a missing URL in footnote 1, typos ('appproximation'), and incomplete sentences in Sec. 3.4.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper clearly formalizes 'elastic models' and Pareto elasticity (Def. 2.1, Eq. 2), identifying a real gap between PEFT/compression methods and the need for smoothly varying deployment budgets.

Strong conceptual contribution: the theory section (Sec. 4) cleanly establishes why post-training selection (Thm. 4.1) and all-subspaces learning (Thm. 4.2) fail, while nested submodel learning recovers the Pareto front (Thm. 4.3). Proofs are provided in App. B and appear correct, including the elegant balanced-factorization penalty (Lemma B.5) and spectral analysis (Lemmas B.6, B.7).

The central approximation (ranking preservation under an additive probe) is not just assumed but empirically validated in an exhaustively searchable setting (App. C.3: Spearman 0.991, 94.1% DP exact-match, low regret), which is unusually rigorous for this type of assumption.

Broad and convincing empirical evaluation spanning GPT-2, the Llama family up to 8B, and DINOv3 ViTs up to 7B, with comparisons to the strongest elastic low-rank baseline (ACIP), other rank-based methods, and methods from other compression families (LLM-Pruner, LayerSkip). The matched-budget comparison against independently trained submodels (Fig. 5) is a particularly fair and informative control.

The Gauge-Aligned Reparametrization (GAR, Sec. 3.5) is a simple but practically valuable trick, and the runtime measurements in App. D.4 confirm the theoretical cost model, addressing the common concern that factorized models don't translate to real speedups.

Good reproducibility posture: code link promised, hyperparameters, datasets, and implementation details are given in App. D; limitations (2x training overhead, no fused kernels, no adaptive routing evaluated) are discussed honestly in Sec. 7.
weaknesses: Inconsistency in describing the controlled validation experiment: Sec. 3.4 describes 'a four-layer network (two CNNs and two MLPs trained on MNIST)' with K^L = 10,000 submodels, while App. D.1 describes a two-layer linear network with no activations and synthetic Gaussian data, and App. C.3 refers to MNIST with 10^4 submodels. This makes the setup for the paper's central validation claim (recovery of the 'true' Pareto front) unclear and should be reconciled.

The theory covers only linear models with Frobenius objectives and additive layer errors; the bridge to deep nonlinear networks rests on the empirical validation, which is conducted only at small scale. The gap between Thm. 4.3's setting and the actual LKD objective (Eq. 5-6) is acknowledged but not quantified at scale.

Baselines are somewhat narrow on the elastic side: ACIP is the only directly comparable prior elastic low-rank method, and FlexTron/LlamaFlex are not compared (justified by unavailability/proprietary data in App. A.1, but still limits external validation of the Pareto claims).

LLM evaluation is limited to zero-shot commonsense tasks via lm-eval-harness (plus LoRA adaptation in Tab. 1); standard perplexity benchmarks for the Llama models are not reported, making cross-paper comparison harder. Post-adaptation results (Tab. 1) show substantial degradation at small budgets (e.g., code accuracy dropping from ~36.8 to ~2.0 at 0.4x), which tempers the 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' claim at aggressive compression.
Several small presentation issues: typos ('appproximation', 'Coincides', 'MNSL'), a missing punctuation in Sec. 3.4, and the 'Impact Statement' is boilerplate.
The nestedness constraint is motivated theoretically but the cost of enforcing it (restricting the reachable configuration set) versus a relaxed constraint is not ablated directly at scale.
